children: Uganda is phasing out Tax Identification Numbers (TINs) in favour of the National Identification Number (NIN), a move the country believes will be critical in widening the tax base.

In a memo issued following the Cabinet meeting on September 1, the government of Uganda said it had resolved to phase out Tax Identification Numbers and adopt National Identification Numbers in their place as a means of streamlining tax administration in the country.

These changes come against the backdrop of a slowdown in the registration of Tax Identification Numbers for individuals, with data from the Uganda Revenue Authority showing that a total of 262,918 Tax Identification Numbers were registered in 2024/25, down from 513,898 in 2021/22.

The country has also reported a decline in the registration of non-individual Tax Identification Numbers, from 21,522 in 2021/22 to 18,023 in 2024/25.“Cabinet has approved the use of National Identification Numbers issued by the National Identification and Registration Authority as Tax Identification Numbers going forward. For years, our tax registration system has relied on separate and largely manual Tax Identification Numbers. It has served its purpose, but it has also left us with outdated and inconsistent records, creating real weaknesses in data accuracy, compliance and service delivery,” the September 1 Cabinet memo states.

The government says the switch will help expand and clean up the tax register by simplifying registration and compliance, as all Ugandans aged 18 and above will effectively be captured in the tax register.
According to data from the Uganda Revenue Authority, the country has a total of 5,251,874 registered taxpayers, up from 2,618,008 in the 2021/22 financial year.

Of the 5,251,874 registered taxpayers, 5,005,075 are individual taxpayers, while the remaining 246,799 are non-individual taxpayers, covering entities such as companies and partnerships.“By adopting the National Identification Number as the Tax Identification Number, we are establishing a consistent identity for every taxpayer. This will improve the accuracy of our taxpayer register, strengthen our ability to identify and trace taxpayers, and make our data systems work better together. It will help us improve compliance, reduce revenue leakage and make it simpler for citizens to register,” the Cabinet memo states.

The switch from Tax Identification Numbers to the National Identification Number for tax administration purposes is the latest in a raft of measures taken by Uganda’s government to boost domestic resource mobilisation.
In mid-August, Uganda joined Tanzania in adopting a staggered approach to the rollout of electronic invoices across the economy.

According to a notice from the Uganda Revenue Authority (URA), the manufacturing, mining, construction, hospitality, real estate and petroleum transportation sectors will be the first to face mandatory electronic invoicing requirements, including businesses whose annual turnover falls below the VAT threshold.“Manufacturing, including the physical or chemical transformation of raw materials or intermediate goods into new products; mining and quarrying, including the extraction of naturally occurring minerals in solid, liquid or gaseous form; water supply, including the collection, treatment and disposal of various forms of waste; and construction, including general and specialised construction of buildings and civil engineering works,” URA states in a notice to the public dated August 10, 2026.

Data from the Uganda Bureau of Statistics show that, in the first three quarters of the 2025/26 financial year, the country collected $6.85 billion in revenue, of which $1.07 billion was attributable to Pay As You Earn (PAYE).
